articles.title: In the digital age, TouchTunes CFO banks on real-life experiences
articles.author: Dan Niepow
articles.content:
Technology may have been Andrew Russakoff’s first and longest love, but finance ended up slotting well into his interests. An engineer by training, Russakoff says he’s been interested in tech all his life. At eight years old, he was already programming computers.
“Studying engineering prepared my brain to work in a way that maps very well to finance,” says Russakoff, who goes by the nickname Rusty.
After earning his engineering degree from Harvard University, he obtained an MBA from Columbia Business School. Following a brief stint in the energy industry, Russakoff spent the heart of his career running finances for IAC, a conglomerate that operates People Magazine and Food & Wine, among other publications. The company, which now goes by People Incorporated, also previously held a stake in Angi, formerly known as Angie’s List.
Russakoff stepped into the CFO seat of digital jukebox operator TouchTunes in April.
In an interview with CFO.com, Russakoff talks through the serendipities that led him from a publicly traded business to a private equity-owned one at TouchTunes, and why he’s bullish on jukeboxes in an increasingly digital age.
Andrew “Rusty” Russakoff
CFO, TouchTunes
First CFO position: June 2022
Notable previous employers:
- IAC, now known as People Inc.
- Angi, formerly known as Angie’s List
Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
DAN NIEPOW: Angi and TouchTunes seem like quite different companies. What attracted you to your latest job at TouchTunes?
ANDREW RUSSAKOFF: It comes down to a few things. First, the unit economics of TouchTunes are very strong. Once a jukebox or a dartboard goes into a venue, it stays there for years. The lifetime of these devices is measured in decades.
Second, living in a world where everybody is worried about AI disruption, I see this as a platform where AI is clearly not a headwind. If anything, it's a tailwind as people are looking for more real-life social connection.
Then finally, there's the asset itself. We have this unparalleled network of connected devices in valuable locations, where prime earning-age adults are spending meaningful blocks of time exposed to our jukeboxes, our dartboards and our mobile app. That's all stitched together through an integrated payment and social experience, and that combination is very compelling to venues as well as to major brands, and overall very hard to replicate.
I’d also add that while TouchTunes and Angi are different, there are some real similarities underneath. TouchTunes has this B2B2C dynamic to it. We make and place connected devices in venues, and then we sell services to consumers through those devices. So, there is this two-sided element to it; it has DNA that is shared with marketplaces, and Angi was a marketplace. Many of the IAC businesses were marketplaces.
This job marks your second CFO position. Looking back, how did you know you were ready to step into the CFO seat in the first place?
I had a very unique and ideal setup to be able to make the transition to CFO. At IAC, I had exposure to almost every experience that goes into being a CFO in my prior financial roles. When the Angi CFO role opened up, I was walking into a company where I already knew the people, the history, the financials and the data.
Usually, you're going into a company where you may not necessarily have any of those things. And then on top of that, I had a safety net of people around me who had put me in a position to succeed.
TouchTunes was purchased by private equity company TA Associates in 2022. You came to the company after working for some publicly traded firms. What’s it been like adjusting to private equity ownership?
One of the things that attracted me to TouchTunes was the people at TA Associates. Meeting them reminded me of some of my early days at IAC, which is a holding company, not a private equity firm, but there are structural parallels.
The culture felt similar because even though IAC is focused on the internet space, in some ways, it's like a value investor in the technology space. TA operates with a patient, long-term mindset, highly aligned with management around growing the value of the company, and that's proven out since I've been here.
Any plans for an IPO at TouchTunes someday?
I wouldn't rule it out, but this business is pretty well set up for the structure that it's in today. It has a resilient, stable and profitable core. That kind of business is naturally appealing to a private equity sponsor.
I could also see TouchTunes being attractive to the right strategic buyer down the road, which could be a public company, or to a company in an adjacent space. Maybe one that’s looking to diversify into a hardware-plus-services platform with a social overlay that's genuinely AI-resilient.
We’re fortunate that there are multiple paths forward; we're focused on building value regardless of which one of them materializes.
TouchTunes now bills itself as “North America's largest connected platform for in-venue social entertainment.” But for those who are familiar with it, the company name only brings to mind jukeboxes. How are you thinking about selling the company to investors and the public at large?
The jukebox serves as the physical anchor for sure, but TouchTunes has evolved itself into far more than a jukebox manufacturer, and into a connected, tech-enabled social entertainment network.
We have a mobile app with a material and significant number of consumers interacting with us and with each other every day. We have an integrated payment system that works across multiple devices and device types within a bar to create a sticky ecosystem and user experience for the venues, the operators, and for the consumers. And we've expanded into adjacent bar sports like the darts business.
We're building overall a scalable digital platform that powers the entire out-of-home social experience, and the story to investors then is about a company that has a scaled installed base, sticky venue relationships, multiple revenue streams and a connected platform that gets more valuable as we add devices, users and data to that ecosystem.
What’s your top TouchTunes song choice?
My favorite TouchTunes memory goes back probably 15 or 20 years, so it's not necessarily a song choice today, but it's a song choice that I made back when digital jukeboxes were first coming onto the scene. I was at a bar with some friends, and I thought it would be funny to cue up the entire Pink Floyd “Animals” album. It was a private joke with the group I was with, but I don't think the rest of the bar shared my enthusiasm.
The funny thing is we actually have features now at TouchTunes to help mitigate that one guy who thinks it's funny to monopolize the whole bar.
articles.summary:
Andrew “Rusty” Russakoff, a former IAC executive, discusses his transition to CFO of TouchTunes and his strategy for growing the digital jukebox operator under private equity ownership.

### Key Points
- Andrew Russakoff joined TouchTunes as CFO in April 2024, following a career at IAC and a previous CFO role at Angi.
- TouchTunes was acquired by the private equity firm TA Associates in 2022.
- The company operates a network of connected in-venue entertainment devices, including digital jukeboxes and dartboards.
- Russakoff highlights the company's B2B2C business model, which combines hardware placement with integrated mobile app and payment services.
- The executive views the platform as AI-resilient, noting that its physical presence in social venues provides a unique, hard-to-replicate market advantage.

### Why it Matters
This leadership transition highlights how established hardware-based businesses are evolving into integrated digital platforms to maintain relevance in a tech-focused market. By leveraging long-term private equity backing, TouchTunes aims to scale its social entertainment network while positioning itself for potential future exit strategies, such as an IPO or a strategic acquisition.

articles.title: Bitcoin tops $80,000: 'Crypto winter is close to being over'
articles.author: Ines Ferré
articles.content:
Investors got a hopeful signal on Thursday that bitcoin (BTC-USD) may defy its historically weak September trend.
The world's largest cryptocurrency jumped more than 5% on Thursday to rise above $81,000 as worries about a Federal Reserve rate hike eased and Treasury yields dropped.
Bitcoin continued to rise on Friday, up 4%.
The question is whether the token can remain above these levels, given that bitcoin has historically posted negative returns in September in nine of the past 15 years.
"It's important data, and we should respect it," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said. However, the strategist noted that the token has "bucked" this historical monthly trend over the past three years.
"We haven't seen a negative September for years, and seasonality — it's a helpful data point, but it is not a foolproof system for trading these markets," he said.
The token is coming off a strong August rally, prompting some strategists to suggest that the crypto bear market may be nearing a bottom if it hasn't already passed it.
"The recent BTC price movement suggests that the crypto winter is close to being over," Noelle Acheson, author of "Crypto Is Macro Now," told Yahoo Finance.
The token rallied 25% last month as the Treasury Department's recent intervention in the bond market and assistance to Japan helped lift the prices of gold and crypto assets.
Some of those gains were given back as oil prices surged and hawkish comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh raised concerns about the Fed's upcoming September rate decision.
On Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller hinted he would support keeping rates unchanged if inflation eases.
"I could see crypto and broader equities mounting a rally post-FOMC that could take bitcoin to a higher level than today into late September, early October, " David Grider, head of liquid investments at Finality Capital, told Yahoo Finance.
Grider said the move would be driven by either a surprise Fed rate hold or by yields falling sharply after the first rate hike.
The risk of a market correction still holds, in which case bitcoin would also be sold off. But crypto analysts see such a move as short-term.
"So long as the Treasury is willing to intervene in the yield curve, we believe, the bid on 'hard assets' such as bitcoin stays," Bernstein analyst Gautam Chhugani wrote in a recent note.
Chhugani and his team called a bottom for bitcoin earlier this year and have placed a $150,000 year-end price target on the token.
With the exception of 2018 and last year, the fourth quarter has proven bullish for bitcoin.
articles.summary:
Bitcoin surged above $81,000 this week as easing Federal Reserve rate hike concerns and falling Treasury yields helped the cryptocurrency defy its historically weak September performance trends.

### Key Points
- Bitcoin prices rose over 5% on Thursday and continued climbing on Friday, reaching levels above $81,000.
- Analysts suggest the recent rally indicates the prolonged "crypto winter" may be nearing an end after a 25% gain in August.
- Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller signaled potential support for keeping interest rates unchanged if inflation data continues to ease.
- Bernstein analysts maintain a $150,000 year-end price target for bitcoin, citing ongoing Treasury interventions in the bond market.
- While September has historically been a negative month for the token, it has bucked that trend for the past three consecutive years.

### Why it Matters
The recent price action suggests that bitcoin is increasingly sensitive to macroeconomic shifts and central bank policy rather than historical seasonal patterns. If the Federal Reserve maintains current rates, the resulting stability could bolster investor confidence in digital assets as a hedge against broader market volatility.

articles.title: Thomson Reuters Court Software Breach May Have Exposed SSNs and Sealed Data
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Thomson Reuters disclosed on Wednesday that an unauthorized party obtained files from C-Track, the court case management platform sold by its West Publishing Corporation unit, in March 2026, affecting courts in 11 U.S. states, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and Ontario, Canada.
West Publishing said it discovered the activity on June 30, 2026. A subset of court records could contain individuals' names, Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, dates of birth, medical information, and health insurance information, the company said.
The firm is offering potentially affected individuals 12 months of Experian IdentityWorks credit monitoring, with enrollment open until December 31, 2026, using a multi-use code published in the notice, and a hotline at 1-833-918-5294 that requires the engagement number B171847.
In Canada, Thomson Reuters Canada Limited is offering 12 months of TransUnion myTrueIdentity monitoring with a call center scheduled to open on September 4.
"Certain confidential, redacted or sealed information may have been impacted for certain affected courts," West Publishing said in its September 2 notice, adding that there is no evidence to date of fraud or misuse of the information.
The West Publishing notice and the Canadian notice from Thomson Reuters Canada Limited name the following court systems -
- Alabama - Alabama Appellate Courts
- Kentucky - Kentucky Appellate Courts
- Montana - Montana Supreme Court
- Nevada - Nevada Appellate Courts
- New Hampshire - The New Hampshire Supreme Court
- North Dakota - North Dakota Supreme Court
- Ohio - First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, Eleventh, and Twelfth District Courts of Appeals
- Pennsylvania - Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Environmental Hearing Board (former client), Court of Common Pleas of Washington County, Fifth Judicial District of Pennsylvania, and the Court of Common Pleas of Monroe County, which the notice lists by county name only
- South Carolina - Supreme Court of South Carolina and the South Carolina Court of Appeals
- Tennessee - Tennessee Appellate Court Clerk's Office
- Wyoming - Wyoming Judicial Branch
- U.S. Virgin Islands - Supreme and Superior Courts
- Ontario - Court of Appeal for Ontario, Ontario Superior Court of Justice, and Ontario Court of Justice
The Hacker News reviewed the West Publishing notice on September 3, 2026; it lists 24 court bodies in 11 states and the U.S. Virgin Islands, with Minnesota absent from the list.
The Minnesota Judicial Branch said on September 2 that data from its appellate courts was exposed in the incident, that it has terminated Thomson Reuters' access to the courts' electronic environments, and that users of the appellate case management system must change their passwords. Minnesota Supreme Court Chief Justice Natalie Hudson said she is "deeply troubled that our court users' data has been compromised."
In Montana Supreme Court's release, the court said the material taken was backup data stored on Thomson Reuters servers, drawn from database copies that had been "supplied to TR for the purpose of troubleshooting the applications."
Those databases may hold case numbers, party names and addresses, phone numbers, the charge and docket entry descriptions, and, for some individuals charged with a crime, driver's license numbers and dates of birth, the release said.
Unauthorized access to that storage location ran from March 1 through June 29, 2026, per the court's account of the vendor's notice.
The Alabama Appellate Courts said West Publishing later told them that a copy of some Alabama appellate court data was kept in a backup file within the company's cloud environment, a backup the courts said they had neither requested nor known about.
"This incident occurred within our vendor's systems, not our own," Alabama Chief Justice Sarah Stewart said.
The Supreme Court of Ohio, however, said in its own statement that Thomson Reuters Court Management Solutions (TRCMS) informed it on August 31 that "the unauthorized access took place on the Court's production platform." That platform hosts the filing system data of the 10 Ohio appellate districts that use C-Track, with the Eighth and Tenth districts unaffected.
The Hacker News has reached out to Thomson Reuters for clarification on which environment was accessed and whether Minnesota courts are affected, and will update this story with any response.
"There has been no operational disruption to C-Track as a result of this incident," a Thomson Reuters spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company considers the platform safe to keep using.
The Supreme Court of Ohio said it has yet to receive comprehensive details of the enhanced security measures TRCMS told it have been deployed.
Ontario's Court of Appeal, Superior Court of Justice, and Court of Justice said in the three chief justices' statement that Thomson Reuters detected the activity within one of its cloud environments. The chief justices said "it is still unclear what information may have been compromised," and that anyone involved in court proceedings or mentioned in court documents could have had personal information involved.
In Wyoming, the material taken was historical data from the Wyoming Supreme Court and district courts, primarily involving people who dealt with those courts between 2015 and 2025, the state's Judicial Branch said in its release.
The preliminary review indicates that "limited personal information, including names, addresses and dates of birth, was compromised," the branch added. Wyoming gives the hotline's hours as 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Mountain Time.
The Virgin Islands courts said they received notice on July 27 and can so far confirm only that the accessed data "related to its 2018 system implementation project."
Trial court e-filing in Kentucky is untouched because the state does not use third-party vendors for it, Kentucky's court administrators said, adding that there is "no indication at this point that the unauthorized third party distributed the Kentucky data."
Montana and Minnesota each said that court documents were not part of the accessed data, although the vendor's notice states that sealed material may have been affected for certain courts.
The vendor notified the courts and Ontario's Ministry of the Attorney General between July 23 and July 27. Public disclosure followed on September 2, a date Montana said was chosen so that the vendor and the other states involved could issue simultaneous announcements.
As of September 3, no party had published a count of affected individuals, the method by which the files were obtained, or the identity of whoever was responsible.
North Dakota's statement said the incident involved only North Dakota Supreme Court data, with the state's district courts and its Odyssey system unaffected. It added that there is no evidence nCourt, the system used to process financial transactions, was impacted.
"There is an active criminal investigation into this incident," the North Dakota Court System said.
articles.summary:
Thomson Reuters disclosed that an unauthorized party accessed sensitive court records from its C-Track management platform, impacting judicial systems across 11 U.S. states, Ontario, and the Virgin Islands.

### Key Points
- Unauthorized access occurred between March 1 and June 29, 2026, involving files stored on Thomson Reuters' cloud and backup servers.
- Compromised data may include Social Security numbers, driver's license details, medical information, and dates of birth.
- Affected jurisdictions include court systems in Alabama, Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Wyoming, and Ontario.
- Thomson Reuters is providing 12 months of credit monitoring services to individuals whose personal information was potentially exposed in the breach.
- Minnesota’s judicial branch terminated its connection to the platform, citing concerns over the exposure of appellate court data.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights significant security risks associated with third-party vendors managing sensitive government and judicial data. The incident raises questions about data retention practices, as several courts reported that the compromised information was stored in backups they were unaware existed.

articles.title: I put Linux on Microsoft’s own hardware, and it somehow works so much better than Windows
articles.author: Amir Bohlooli
articles.content:
You've heard the advice. I have too. In fact, I've even given it. Heck, I've even followed said advice, on numerous occasions. What advice? Ah, yes. The "just install Linux" advice.
I had a Dell Latitude that I bought used. It came with Windows 10, then spent some time as a headless Ubuntu server, and when I eventually built a proper homelab, I installed Ubuntu Desktop on it instead. It works so, so smoothly.
That successful installation was still lingering in the back of my head when I saw an old Microsoft Surface Pro 6 lying around. It's my dad's, and he mainly uses it as a tablet with the Surface Pen for writing.
The problem was that this Microsoft device could barely hold a charge, got ridiculously hot, and was laggy all the time. Windows just wasn't working particularly well on this Surface. So... can we put Linux on a Microsoft Surface? A device that was literally made for Windows?
Yes, you can put Linux on a Surface
"You can install Linux on anything"
Of course you can. The more nuanced question is whether everything will actually work afterward.
I'll spare you the platitude, but Linux really has come a long way. After all, the year of the Linux desktop is coming (any day now!) We've even got gamers, of all people, switching to Linux on their PCs. So why not a Surface?
A Surface packs quite a bit of hardware that falls outside what you'd expect from an ordinary laptop: there's a touchscreen. There are two cameras, in addition to the Windows Hello IR camera. There's the Surface Pen. Depending on the model, there are all sorts of sensors and other Microsoft-specific hardware to worry about.
|  | 
| A cute message I got from the Surface Pro as I was very vigorously trying to shut it down. | 
Some hardware simply does not work properly on Linux. But lo and behold, there's an entire project dedicated to making Linux work on Surface devices.
Linux-surface provides a customized kernel and drivers to get Surface hardware running properly under Linux. In theory, you can install just about any distro on a Surface, set up linux-surface, and start tinkering. In practice, the project provides straightforward installation instructions for the usual mainstream distros: buntu, Debian, Fedora, and Arch-based systems.
So, install a distro, set up linux-surface, fiddle with whatever breaks, and eventually I should have a working Linux Surface. But I wanted it even easier. Could it get easier?
Ultramarine basically does the work for you
Thankfully, we're not the first people to want this
Take roughly what Linux Mint does for Ubuntu and apply that philosophy to Fedora. You get something along the lines of Ultramarine Linux.
It's essentially Fedora with a bunch of useful extras already baked in. More importantly for me, Ultramarine offers a Surface image that already includes linux-surface and the extra drivers and codecs needed for Microsoft's hardware.
You can download the image from Ultramarine's website. It comes with four desktop environments: KDE Plasma, Xfce, Budgie, and GNOME. I went with KDE Plasma.
The installation is, thanks to the wonderful age of GUI installers, very simple and straightforward. Getting the live USB to actually boot was a little less straightforward.
Secure Boot had other plans
The first time I booted from the USB, I got GRUB (great!) Then I selected Ultramarine and immediately got an error saying the kernel was missing (not great!)
The problem, as you may have guessed, was Secure Boot. I went into the Surface's UEFI settings, disabled Secure Boot, and tried booting the USB again. This time, instead of Linux, I got a blue screen demanding my BitLocker recovery key (also not great!)
I had completely forgotten about Windows device encryption. This Surface Pro 6 had been running Windows 11 Home, where encryption can be enabled automatically without you knowing.
Fortunately, the fix was more annoying than difficult. I grabbed the recovery key from my Microsoft account, typed in the 48 digits, changed the boot order so I could get back into Windows, suspended the encryption protection from PowerShell, and rebooted.
I say "suspended" because fully decrypting the drive would have taken considerably longer. And in this case, there wasn't much point. The next time this Surface booted from its SSD, Windows wasn't going to be there anymore anyway. After that, Ultramarine finally booted.
Linux made the Surface chill out
Most of the important stuff just works
Speakers, touchscreen, microphone, and cameras all worked immediately. Not a single terminal command was required to get any of them working. The Surface Pen connected and worked too, which was especially important considering that's basically the whole reason my dad uses this thing.
This sounds like the setup for me to now list everything that didn't work. Well... it is.
Alas, the Windows Hello IR camera does not work! I'm not even going to bother fighting that battle. It's a sacrifice I'm OK with. The regular cameras also aren't exactly perfect. The image is very dark and clearly needs some tuning. But hey, this is Linux we're talking about. I can dig into the configuration and tweak it however I like. Even make it look better than Windows Camera did.
The important peripherals work, though, and the difference was soon noticeable. The Surface runs much cooler now. I haven't heard the fan spin up once since switching to Linux, whereas Windows would make them run minutes after boot.
I'll eventually install my usual collection of open-source software and it'll start feeling like home pretty quickly. There is, however, one area where Windows still has the advantage.
Windows still knows it's a tablet
KDE isn't quite there yet
I've complained plenty in the past about Microsoft seemingly optimizing Windows 11 for an imaginary audience of tablet users. Well, ladies and gentlemen, I found the tablet user. It's me.
All that extra spacing, padding, oversized buttons, and touch-friendly UI suddenly makes much more sense when you're actually using Windows 11 on a touchscreen without a keyboard attached.
KDE Plasma does an OK job here. The on-screen keyboard pops up when I need it, and basic touch navigation works well enough. But it isn't elegant. The interface doesn't transform when I detach the Type Cover. There's no convincing equivalent of Windows recognizing that it's suddenly a tablet and adapting itself accordingly.
You can definitely use KDE with touch. I have been. But, it will still feel like operating a desktop interface with fingers rather than using an interface designed around them. That's probably the biggest compromise I've found so far.
I expected a project, not an upgrade
I went into this expecting Linux on a Surface Pro to be one of those fun (?) weekend projects. You know, the ones where you spend six hours fixing drivers, get 80% of the hardware working, declare victory, and then reinstall Windows three days later... That isn't what happened.
Ultramarine booted, the important Surface hardware worked, the Pen worked, and the machine became cooler and noticeably more pleasant to use. Even the pressure input from the pen worked. The biggest issue I've run into wasn't the kernel, which in itself is a blessing. It's that KDE isn't quite as comfortable on a tablet as Windows 11. That's a remarkably good problem to have. I have an array of Linux environments to choose from.
I wouldn't tell every Surface owner to immediately wipe Windows and install Linux. Windows still has better integration with some of the hardware, especially if things like Windows Hello and a polished tablet UI matter to you.
But if you've got an older Surface that's getting hot, sluggish, and increasingly unpleasant to use, I wouldn't write the hardware off just yet.
The solution to my aging Microsoft tablet was exactly the same nearly annoying advice everyone drops in the comments sections: just install Linux, bro.
articles.summary:
Installing Ultramarine Linux on an aging Microsoft Surface Pro 6 improves thermal performance and system responsiveness, offering a viable alternative to Windows for users with older, sluggish hardware.

### Key Points
- The linux-surface project provides a customized kernel and drivers to ensure compatibility between Microsoft hardware and various Linux distributions.
- Ultramarine Linux offers a pre-configured installation image that includes the necessary drivers and codecs for Surface devices, simplifying the setup process.
- Essential hardware, including the touchscreen, speakers, microphone, and Surface Pen, functions immediately upon installation without requiring manual terminal configuration.
- Users must disable Secure Boot and manage BitLocker encryption keys within the UEFI settings to successfully boot from external installation media.
- While performance is improved, the Windows Hello IR camera remains unsupported, and desktop environments like KDE Plasma lack the native tablet-mode optimizations found in Windows 11.

### Why it Matters
Transitioning older Surface devices to Linux can extend the hardware's lifespan by reducing thermal output and eliminating the performance lag often associated with aging Windows installations. While users may sacrifice specific proprietary features like Windows Hello, the improved system stability provides a practical solution for those looking to repurpose legacy tablets.

articles.title: Trump Taking Stake In Corporations Opens Door For Dems To Exploit When They Regain Power
articles.author: Jack McGeever
articles.content:
President Donald Trump’s growing push to take government stakes in private companies could hand Democrats a powerful precedent to expand federal involvement in corporate America when they return to power.
The Trump administration has announced 39 stakes or other ownership rights in private companies totaling roughly $27.7 billion since January 2025, spanning the mining, technology, energy and defense industries, according to Politico. The left is already considering how a future Democratic administration could build on Trump’s approach to advance climate, energy and labor priorities, while free-market advocates warned the president has made it more difficult for Republicans to oppose such interventions in the future. (RELATED: Trump’s Intel Deal Could Set Problematic Precedent Dems Can Exploit)
The administration’s approach marked a significant departure from previous federal interventions in private companies, which largely occurred during wars or financial emergencies. The federal government took large stakes in banks and automakers during the 2008 financial crisis, but Trump’s investments have instead been aimed at longer-term efforts to secure critical mineral supply chains and expand domestic semiconductor and technology production.
Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, told the Daily Caller News Foundation that Trump’s acquisition of a 10% stake in Intel represented a significant escalation from earlier government investments.
Lincicome said previous government stakes generally involved national security needs or emergencies, received legislative backing and included plans for the government to eventually divest. The Intel deal, by contrast, involved a company that was not facing bankruptcy, lacked an explicit exit strategy and relied on the CHIPS Act, which Lincicome said did not expressly authorize the government to take an equity stake.
“Because the Trump administration has opened these floodgates, it’s going to be difficult, if not impossible, for Republicans to fight this when Trump is gone,” Lincicome told the DCNF. “Because it was their party that started it all.”
Former President Joe Biden signed the CHIPS and Science Act into law in 2022 to boost domestic semiconductor manufacturing and reduce U.S. reliance on foreign chip production. The law included roughly $52 billion in subsidies for semiconductor manufacturers, along with additional funding for scientific and technology research. (RELATED: Trump Admin To Tech Companies: Give Us Ownership And We’ll Give You Funding)
The White House rejected concerns that Democrats would build on Trump’s approach, arguing the administration’s investments were voluntary partnerships intended to strengthen American industry.
“The Trump administration has taken voluntary equity investments in willing companies,” White House spokesman Kush Desai told the DCNF. “After spending decades hollowing America out with broken trade deals and DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] red tape, it’s unlikely Democrats will want to build on the President’s legacy of partnering with the private sector to reindustrialize the United States.”
Left-wing policy groups, however, have already begun considering how a future administration could use government ownership for its own priorities. A July Roosevelt Institute report laid out a potential 2029 climate agenda that explicitly called for adapting Trump’s methods to advance the left’s goals and identified government stakes in private companies as one tool future policymakers could use. The report argued government ownership could be used to push companies toward faster decarbonization, union recognition, domestic production and restrictions on stock buybacks.
Former Biden administration National Economic Council deputy director Bharat Ramamurti also predicted a future Democratic president would inherit the stakes.
“Inevitably a Democratic president is going to get handed these equity stakes at some point,” Ramamurti told Politico, adding that the next administration would have to determine what to do with them.
The concept has already attracted prominent figures on the left. California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed a national public equity fund that would give Americans a stake in wealth generated by major artificial intelligence companies, while independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced legislation in June that would give the public a 50% ownership stake in the country’s largest AI companies.
Lincicome warned that the political precedent was only one risk created by expanding government ownership, arguing the investments could distort capital markets by encouraging investors to bet on which companies might receive government support rather than which businesses have the strongest commercial prospects.
“The U.S. economy dominates in large part because capital flows to the best ideas and the best companies, not to the ones that are coziest with the government,” Lincicome told the DCNF.
articles.summary:
The Trump administration’s acquisition of $27.7 billion in private company stakes across multiple industries has established a precedent that could enable future Democratic administrations to expand federal corporate influence.

### Key Points
- Since January 2025, the Trump administration has secured 39 ownership stakes in mining, technology, energy, and defense firms.
- The government acquired a 10% stake in Intel, a move critics note lacks an explicit exit strategy or the emergency context typical of past federal interventions.
- Investments are largely facilitated through the CHIPS and Science Act, which provides $52 billion in subsidies to boost domestic semiconductor manufacturing.
- Left-leaning policy groups and politicians, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Governor Gavin Newsom, are exploring how to leverage these ownership models for climate and labor goals.
- Economists warn that these interventions may distort capital markets by prioritizing companies with government ties over those with the strongest commercial performance.

### Why it Matters
This shift in federal policy fundamentally alters the relationship between the government and the private sector by normalizing state ownership outside of traditional financial crises. By establishing this framework, the current administration may inadvertently provide a roadmap for future leaders to exert direct control over corporate operations and industrial priorities.

articles.title: The Fight for Serious AI Regulation Just Won a Big Victory in Massachusetts
articles.author: John Nichols
articles.content:
The Fight for Serious AI Regulation Just Won a Big Victory in Massachusetts
After his primary win, Ed Markey says he’s ready to take on “the criminal enterprises” of Big Tech.
Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey won a major primary election victory on Tuesday, claiming another win for the left in this summer’s struggle for the soul of the Democratic Party. “Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey declared to a cheering crowd in which his young supporters celebrated a 65–35 triumph over his primary rival, US Representative Seth Moulton.
It was also, the senator explained, a victory in the fight against what he described as “the criminal enterprises of Big Oil and Big Tech.” A longtime foe of corporate greed and monopoly, Markey made stymieing the plans of AI oligarchs a crucial part of his campaign. With progressive-populist enthusiasm, he promised to “tax the rich, block the bombs, and stop data centers from polluting our communities.”
This is not a new fight for Markey. As the senator noted earlier this year, he’s been “working for more than a decade to propose commonsense policies to take back unchecked power from Big Tech and put it into the hands of the American people.”
But what made Markey’s victory notable was that, in the last days of the primary campaign, he faced and overcame a cynical attack from Moulton, who attempted to dumb down the AI debate in a way that he thought would turn voters against the incumbent.
Moulton’s primary challenge to Markey was always tough to fathom. A middle-aged congressman with limitless ambition but finite political skills—as evidenced by his failed bid for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination—Moulton tried to make the fight a generational struggle between a 47-year-old rival and an 80-year-old incumbent. The message never got traction because Markey campaigned relentlessly as an energetic progressive legislator with a record of standing on the right side of history.
Yet Moulton’s desperation to make the race a referendum on youth-versus-age made the last days before Tuesday’s primary contest an instructive measure of the emerging discourse over AI regulation.
When the two candidates clashed in a pre-primary debate last month, Markey gave an uninspired answer to a silly question about whether he uses AI tools on his electronic devices. He basically said he used the apps that were on his iPhone and iPad and left it at that.
Moulton, who talked during the campaign about “winning the AI race while making sure our kids, our economy, and our communities are protected,” seized on what he thought was an opening to catch up with an incumbent who was opening a wide lead in the polls. “Not understanding the basics of AI—the most important technology of our lifetime—should be disqualifying for a U.S. Senator,” he announced on social media. “This is why we need a new generation of leadership. The future is now.”
Then he pinned the message to the top of his X feed. Then he made a campaign ad. Then the challenger said, “Americans are genuinely concerned about AI. Octogenarians in the Senate are not helping.”
The campaigns also traded charges about Moulton’s investment in defense contractors, including “an AI firm that partners with the U.S. Army,” and how Markey had received the support of a nonprofit backed by Anthropic, a firm that has supported AI regulation
Amid all this bluster, Markey kept his cool, while Moulton revealed his naïveté regarding the debate over AI.
That debate is about a lot more than ruminations on the relative merits of ChatGPT and Claude. It is a fight over who will set the rules for our future.
The mounting pressure to meet the demands of the AI billionaires—to whom Donald Trump pays so much deference—raises fundamental questions about corporate power, privacy, the future of work, and a host of other issues. These are issues that Markey—long a leading Senate advocate for worker rights and consumer protection—has been focused on for years. And they are issues on which he has displayed far more insight and agility than most members of Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Markey’s detailed “AI Accountability Agenda: Taking Power Back From Big Tech” program pulls together groundbreaking legislative proposals to regulate data centers and to address the broader impacts of AI—including the No Robot Bosses Act, which “would prohibit an employer from primarily relying on automated systems for work-related decisions such as hiring, firing, or promotion. The legislation would also require employers to disclose to their employees their use of an automated decision system; conduct detailed evaluations of an automated system’s impact on workers before using the system; and provide an employee with the option to appeal to a human any decision involving an automated system.”
The senator has also proposed and supported legislation to create a human override option for AI decisions that might limit access to healthcare, infringe on privacy rights, or endanger children, and to prevent AI-powered algorithms from amplifying the biases and discrimination that is already embedded in society.
Markey’s even got a plan to prevent the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of AI oligarchs. His Equal Tax Act “would tax investment income at the same rate as ordinary labor income for individuals making more than $1 million. The bill would limit preferential tax rates for long-term capital gains and dividends, end the stepped-up basis loophole, restrict the use of like-kind exchanges by the ultra-wealthy, and limit the passthrough deduction for high-income individuals. By closing loopholes that reward wealth over work, the Equal Tax Act would ensure that the people who profit most from the AI boom pay their fair share.”
Voters recognize that the fight over AI cannot be reduced to election-eve jibes over which candidate might more ably manipulate apps on a phone. It is an existential struggle over questions of whether those with wealth and power will roll over workers, consumers, and civil rights. “Americans,” Markey has explained, “deserve policymakers who are paying attention to their lives, not Big Tech’s bottom line.” By an overwhelming margin, Massachusetts voters gave Ed Markey a mandate to continue serving as that sort of policymaker.
articles.summary:
Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey secured a decisive primary victory, reinforcing his legislative commitment to aggressive AI regulation and curbing the unchecked power of major technology corporations.

### Key Points
- Senator Ed Markey defeated Representative Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts primary with a 65–35 margin.
- Markey’s "AI Accountability Agenda" includes the No Robot Bosses Act, which restricts the use of automated systems in workplace hiring and firing decisions.
- The senator advocates for legislation requiring human override options for AI decisions affecting healthcare, privacy, and child safety.
- Markey’s proposed Equal Tax Act aims to increase taxes on investment income for high earners to prevent the concentration of wealth among AI industry leaders.
- The campaign highlighted tensions regarding corporate influence, with debates focusing on data center regulation and the ethical implications of automated decision-making.

### Why it Matters
This election result signals strong voter support for a regulatory approach that prioritizes worker protections and consumer rights over the interests of major technology firms. It establishes a clear political mandate for federal oversight of AI development and corporate accountability in the digital economy.

articles.title: LA for showbiz, NYC for finance: talent clusters still matter in a world shrunk by telecom connectivity
articles.author: mint
articles.content:
Even more so than usual, Hollywood’s future is uncertain. For decades the Los Angeles economy revolved around the film industry, but now more movies and shows are filmed elsewhere, driven or lured away by high expenses or tax incentives. The prospect of Paramount leaving California over the state’s antitrust lawsuit may not be serious, but the very idea that it can be entertained shows how much the economics of the industry have changed.
Los Angeles is not the only US city being forced to consider a future without the industry that has defined its identity. Over the last half century, if you worked in tech, the Bay Area was the place to be, with access to top talent and financing. If you wanted to become a finance master-of-the-universe, you needed to at least start your career in New York. Now all of this is changing—with implications not only for these cities but also for the US economy.
Success didn’t necessarily require living in one of these cities—but it made success more likely, so the best talent clustered in them. These clusters created an ecosystem that generated well-paid jobs and job growth. There was spillover into other industries and more innovation.
Clusters also made US films, tech and finance the best in the world. When an industry is mostly located in one place, people can more easily build networks, compare notes and develop skills. They can job hop and share know-how. Talent from all over the world comes to that one place, creating positive externalities.
A big part of the US technology industry’s success—and America’s lead in innovation—is due to the fact that it is located in Silicon Valley. That conferred benefits on the larger economy, because it has fostered innovation in all industries, not to mention greater tax revenue and a booming stock market. Other cities tried to start their own tech clusters, but none could match Silicon Valley; once a cluster gets that critical mass of top talent, it is very difficult to displace.
The pandemic challenged that stickiness. First, it became more acceptable to work from home, and once Zoom meetings became normalized, people could work from anywhere. Second, for a while cities were unpleasant places to live, with a spike in crime and a decline in quality of life. Since the pandemic, affordability has become a bigger issue, with rising inflation and home prices. Then, among the very wealthy, there were a few notable moves to Florida and Texas.
But cluster cities have endured.
Citadel is still making a major investment in New York because the benefits of being in the world’s financial capital still outweigh the costs. The Bay Area, meanwhile, remains the place where the big AI firms are headquartered and deals are done. Relocating a major studio from Los Angeles might be possible, but it would not be easy because so much of the film industry is still there.
On an individual level, if you are established in your career, maybe you can move out of a cluster. But if you are just beginning or want to start a new business, living in a cluster is still important.
Politicians in cluster cities seem to be counting on their continued stickiness. California may pass a wealth tax that will hit tech founders especially hard. LA remains an expensive place to do business.
The mayor of New York has not exactly fostered a business-friendly environment (and seems to realize it). Underperforming schools and quality of life around homelessness and petty crime remain unaddressed in cluster cities. Local politicians talk a lot about affordability, but their actual policies will not solve the problems making things more expensive.
A central lesson from economics is that behaviour on the margins is often revealing about what is happening in an economy. There is still value to living in a cluster city—but if the costs rise and the benefits diminish, that calculation changes.
For some people, it already has. Smaller clusters in other cities are becoming more viable, especially for anyone somewhat established who is raising a family. You can work in film in Atlanta or finance in Texas because there is a critical mass of talent there too.
Cluster cities will not necessarily become ‘the next Detroit,’ because their industries will still generate jobs and money. They may even still dominate—just not as much as they used to. That will mean less tax revenue, worse public services, and more economic populism.
De-clustering would also slow the rate of innovation, making the entire US economy less competitive.
There is a magic that comes from having a lot of talented people in one place, and that magic remains critical to the modern American economy. ©Bloomberg
The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering economics.
articles.summary:
The traditional dominance of major American industry hubs like Los Angeles, Silicon Valley, and New York is shifting as rising costs and remote work encourage talent to relocate.

### Key Points
- High costs, tax incentives in other regions, and remote work trends are challenging the long-standing economic dominance of traditional industry clusters.
- Silicon Valley remains the primary hub for global AI innovation, while New York continues to attract major financial firms like Citadel despite affordability concerns.
- Emerging secondary hubs, such as Atlanta for film and Texas for finance, are gaining viability as talent seeks alternatives to expensive coastal cities.
- California’s proposed wealth taxes and quality-of-life issues in major cities are testing the "stickiness" that has historically kept top talent and businesses concentrated.
- Economic clusters provide unique benefits, including professional networking, knowledge sharing, and innovation, which are difficult to replicate in decentralized environments.

### Why it Matters
The potential decline of these industry clusters could reduce tax revenues and public service quality in major cities while slowing the pace of national innovation. If the United States loses its ability to concentrate top talent, the broader economy may become less competitive on the global stage.

articles.title: Apple Reportedly Planning All-New MacBook Model Between Air and Pro
articles.author: Tim Hardwick
articles.content:
Apple may introduce an entirely new 13.8-inch OLED MacBook model in 2029, potentially creating a new product tier between the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro, according to an updated product roadmap from research firm Omdia.
The firm's latest roadmap sandwiches a new 13.8-inch MacBook between the projected time line for the Air and Pro models. The surprise model is said to use a single-stack hybrid OLED panel, rather than the more sophisticated tandem OLED technology that is expected in the upcoming OLED MacBook Pro models, which are set to launch either later this year or early next year.
It seems this prediction hasn't come out of nowhere, either. According to a June report from ZDNet Korea, Apple sounded out Samsung Display, LG Display, and BOE for information regarding a 13.8-inch OLED MacBook panel earlier this year. At the time, the general assumption was that it was likely to be part of Apple's work on the first OLED MacBook Air, expected by 2028 at the earliest.
However, looking at Omdia's latest roadmap, the OLED MacBook Air is conspicuously absent, having been replaced by the 13.8-inch OLED machine in a separate "new" product category. The new model is expected to incorporate an LTPO+ backplane, integrated touch sensing, an under-panel camera, and a color filter integrated into the OLED encapsulation layer.
Omdia believes it is still too early to know for sure which display manufacturer would supply panels for the device, but the firm believes that it could potentially become an important mainstream MacBook product, positioned between the LCD MacBook Air and the higher-end OLED MacBook Pro.
Meanwhile, the MacBook Air line is shown as continuing to use LCD displays right into 2030.
Of course, Apple's wholesale OLED adoption plans could change, and Omdia itself caveats that its roadmap is based on current market expectations. On that basis alone, it could be adjusted at any time according to OLED manufacturing capacity, component costs, and Apple's wider product strategy. Additionally, this is the first we've heard of a completely new MacBook line, and it's still three years out. So with all due caution, file this one under "wait and see."
articles.summary:
Apple is reportedly planning to launch a new 13.8-inch OLED MacBook model by 2029, potentially establishing a distinct product tier positioned between the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.

### Key Points
- Research firm Omdia projects the new 13.8-inch laptop will feature a single-stack hybrid OLED panel with an LTPO+ backplane.
- The device is expected to include advanced hardware features such as integrated touch sensing, an under-panel camera, and an integrated color filter.
- Apple has reportedly consulted display manufacturers Samsung Display, LG Display, and BOE regarding the production of these specific 13.8-inch panels.
- The roadmap suggests the standard MacBook Air line will continue utilizing LCD display technology through 2030.
- This potential product category remains subject to change based on future manufacturing capacity, component costs, and Apple's evolving hardware strategy.

### Why it Matters
This development signals a potential shift in Apple’s hardware strategy by creating a new mid-range tier that bridges the gap between consumer and professional laptop offerings. If realized, this move could influence future display supply chain investments and redefine the standard features expected in mainstream portable computing.

articles.title: Xiaomi makes a huge splash at IFA, shows off upcoming Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor and futuristic AI capabilities
articles.author: derrek.lee@futurenet.com (Derrek Lee) , Derrek Lee
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Xiaomi is making its debut at IFA, with its first major presence at the trade show and the largest event space it's held overseas.
- Xiaomi is highlighting its Human x Car x Home portfolio, which includes more than 300 devices, from smart home appliances to cars.
- The company also showcased the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold, a wide foldable that will rival the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
Xiaomi is making its debut at IFA with an exhibition space that is its largest overseas space to date. The company is using up a whopping 3,300 square meters to showcase hundreds of products in its Human x Car x Home portfolio, from concepts to devices available today, with a focus on how these devices will connect with you throughout your life, both at home and in your car.
Curiously, the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold is among those devices showcased at IFA, with the official launch already set for September 7.
"This year's IFA marks a significant milestone in Xiaomi's global journey," says Xiaomi CMO Xu Fei in a statement.
"Over the years, we have expanded from smartphones into smart home and smart vehicles, while investing deeply in foundational technologies including AI, operating systems, chips and smart manufacturing.
Today, these businesses and capabilities are coming together through our 'Human × Car × Home' smart ecosystem, which we are presenting at scale to a global audience at IFA."
If you're familiar with Xiaomi and its smartphones, you may already know that the company also produces a line of home appliances and smart home devices, including TVs, smart lights, cameras, and more. What you may not know is that Xiaomi also builds cars, like the SU7 Max and YU7, and the groundwork for a wholly interconnected smart home ecosystem lies behind many of these products.
The Human x Car x Home ecosystem is powered by HyperOS, the backbone of Xiaomi's product portfolio, which lets Xiaomi lay the foundation for a seamless AI experience across devices, which it is showing off at IFA through future concepts and today's use cases.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
For example, while you're driving home, AI can gather contextual weather information to ensure your home's lighting and air conditioning are set before you arrive. And this interconnectivity doesn't stop there, with Xiaomi showcasing many ways its ecosystem can work across devices for whatever you need.
This includes its Android smartphones, such as the Xiaomi 17 Ultra and the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold, a wide foldable that closely follows in the footsteps of the popular Galaxy Z Fold 8 and is powered by the company's in-house XRING 03 chipset, enhanced for on-device AI.
Xiaomi hasn't revealed much about this new phone (yet), though it has a triple-camera system on the back and a striking deep red color. It also promises to be very performant, thanks to Xiaomi's new chip, which could rival the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Apple's latest silicon.
Still, we don't have to wait too long for answers, with the launch just days away.
Android Central's take
I'm on the ground at IFA 2026, and Xiaomi's event space is truly a sight to behold. There's a lot to do and see, but perhaps the thing I'm most interested in is the Xiaomi 18 Fold. For one, it looks like Xiaomi is simplifying its foldable naming convention. However, the Fold is coming at a time when Samsung is reinvigorating the foldable space with its own wide foldable.
Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 appears to be incredibly popular, and I understand why. I was shocked by how much I liked it during my hands-on time, and that feeling remained throughout my review, where I've even begun to question my allegiance to flip phones.
The Xiaomi 18 Fold already appears to have a leg up over Samsung, sporting three rear cameras instead of two, although it will be important to see how Xiaomi prices it. We also don't know if or when it will be available globally.

He's been obsessed with mobile technology since he was 12, when he discovered the Nokia N90, and his love of flip phones and new form factors continues to this day. As a fitness enthusiast, he has always been curious about the intersection of tech and fitness. When he's not working, he's probably working out.

Xiaomi is making its major debut at IFA 2026, showcasing its expansive Human x Car x Home ecosystem and the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold foldable smartphone to global audiences.

### Key Points
- Xiaomi occupies a 3,300-square-meter exhibition space at IFA, marking its largest overseas presence to date.
- The company is highlighting its Human x Car x Home portfolio, which integrates over 300 devices through the HyperOS platform.
- The upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold features a triple-camera system and is powered by the proprietary XRING 03 chipset.

articles.title: Nvidia Launches Free Tool That Links Idle Computers Into a Personal AI Data Center
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.content:
Nvidia has launched PAIR, a free open-source tool that links compatible computers on a home network so they can pool idle processing power for local AI inference and agentic workloads. "While the compatible devices are mostly Nvidia GeForce GPUs (PAIR works with RTX 20-series cards and newer, as well as RTX Pro GPUs and DGX Spark systems), Apple's M4 chips or newer will also work," reports The Verge. From the report:  The key thing here is that PAIR uses your in-home systems when they're idle to avoid interfering with other tasks. And this disaggregated system of computers can work in parallel to chew through lots of processing requests -- which should be helpful for an agentic workflow that breaks complex tasks into smaller jobs. This should prevent large bottlenecks on a single GPU, and Nvidia says PAIR can adapt as devices join or leave the network -- including if a user does something like start playing a game on their desktop PC.

articles.title: The first thing Apple’s new CEO did was rename a Canadian lake
articles.author: Ana Maria Constantin
articles.content:
John Ternus became chief executive of Apple on Tuesday. The first public decision of his tenure was to rename a Canadian lake. It was also not his decision to make.
Apple Maps now shows Lake Ontario as “Lake America” to users in the United States. Mark Gurman reported the change for Bloomberg on Tuesday evening. Canadian users still see Lake Ontario. Everyone else sees both. The rollout began on Ternus’s first day and was still spreading across desktop and mobile on Wednesday.
Who actually made the call
Tim Cook stood down as chief executive on Monday, but he did not leave. He is now executive chairman. Bloomberg reports that he keeps responsibility for Apple’s relationship with the White House and with other governments.
That matters here more than anywhere. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox Business on Monday that President Donald Trump had “reached out to Apple directly”. The request therefore arrived at the top of the company, on the day the top changed hands. It landed in a portfolio the outgoing chief executive still holds.
We reported on Tuesday that Ternus also inherits a services chief with more of Apple under him than anyone except the new boss.
Apple declined to comment to Bloomberg and has said nothing publicly about why it made the change. The succession we reported on Tuesday was framed around products and artificial intelligence. This was the part nobody put in a memo.
What Trump ordered
Trump signed the executive order on 27 August, days after trade talks with Canada collapsed. It gives the Interior Department 30 days to change the name in the Geographic Names Information System. That federal database sets the standards for official US maps.
The order reaches federal agencies and nothing else. It cannot bind Canada, other countries, individual US states, or private companies. New York’s governor Kathy Hochul has said her state will keep calling it Lake Ontario.
The dispute underneath it is tariffs. Washington has imposed 50% duties on $20bn of Canadian goods, and Ottawa has promised dollar-for-dollar retaliation.
Google went first, on 29 August, citing its long-standing policy of following official government sources. Apple has never explained its reasoning at all. Both companies renamed the Gulf of Mexico last year on the same basis, and Mexico sued Google over it.
The company that said no is winning
MapQuest refused. “We’re not changing it,” the company posted. It then rebuilt the tool it made during the Gulf of Mexico row, which lets people rename the lake themselves.
The response was extraordinary for a 30-year-old service most people had written off. Appfigures recorded roughly 80,000 iOS downloads across the US and Canada on Sunday. The daily average earlier in August was about 500. Google Play went from around 1,000 a day to 20,000 on Saturday.
Sensor Tower put global downloads at 184,000 for the week beginning 24 August. That is more than ten times the week before. MapQuest says usage climbed to about 50 times normal levels, and that 30 August was its best day in a decade.
It reached number one among free apps in both the US and Canadian App Stores, as Sarah Perez reported for TechCrunch. Doug Berger, its general manager, said people had spoken with their downloads and wanted a map with names they recognised.
The irony is not small. MapQuest sits at the top of Apple’s own App Store because it refused to do what Apple did.
The name Apple replaced
Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes and the name is older than either country. It appears in the records of the Second Continental Congress in 1776, a week after the colonies declared independence, and in the Treaty of Paris that ended the war in 1783.
Accounts of its origin differ. Prime Minister Mark Carney traced it to the Wendat word Ontarí:io, which he rendered as “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big”. Other accounts give the Huron oniatarí:io as “lake of shining waters”, or the Haudenosaunee Skanadario as “beautiful water”. What is not disputed is that the name is Indigenous and predates the province it is often assumed to be named after.
Three of the five Great Lakes carry Indigenous names. Huron and Superior are French.
Canada is not playing
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario, then, now and always,” Carney wrote.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford compared the order to a sketch show and had a physical sign installed at the lake reading “Lake Ontario. Now and Always”. Trump has posted AI-generated video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that most Americans oppose the change. Canada has answered in other ways too, with reports of shops and streets quietly dropping American names as the trade fight drags on.
What it costs to comply
Apple has spent this week under closer scrutiny than usual. It handed over the chief executive’s office and set Ternus’s pay at a $3m salary against a $55m equity target. It holds its first event of the new era on 9 September, where a foldable iPhone is expected.
Into that week it inserted a decision with no product logic and no stated reasoning, on a request that arrived from the president personally, in an area the previous chief executive still runs. Google at least published a policy to point at. Apple published nothing.
The measurable result so far is that a mapping service nobody had thought about since the 1990s is the most downloaded free app in two countries.

articles.summary:
Apple has updated its Maps application to label Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for U.S. users following a direct request from President Donald Trump amid ongoing trade tensions.

### Key Points
- Apple implemented the name change on the first day of John Ternus’s tenure as CEO, though the request was handled by executive chairman Tim Cook.
- The change follows an August 27 executive order from President Trump requiring federal agencies to update the Geographic Names Information System.
- Google previously updated its maps to reflect the name change on August 29, citing its policy of following official U.S. government data.
- MapQuest refused to adopt the new name, resulting in a surge of over 180,000 downloads and reaching the top of the App Store charts.
- The name "Ontario" is of Indigenous origin, predating the formation of both the United States and Canada.

### Why it Matters
This move highlights the complex intersection of corporate governance, geopolitical pressure, and the influence of government mandates on private technology platforms. The resulting consumer backlash and the sudden resurgence of a legacy competitor demonstrate the potential reputational risks companies face when aligning digital products with controversial political directives.
